7.content:
College student Stefani (Kaitlyn Santa Juana) dreams of hundreds of strangers dying. But the real threat is closer to home as the Grim Reaper goes after her family.

You don’t need ESP to know that _Final Destination Bloodlines_ will start with a premonition. And this one’s a belter, eclipsing the plane crash (1), rollercoaster derailment (3), speedway crash (4) and suspension bridge collapse (5) that have previously acted as the franchise’s gory-glory curtain-raisers. Heck, it perhaps even rivals [the second instalment](https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/final-destination-2-review/)’s Route 2 pile-up that made driving behind a logging truck such a no-no for all right-minded motorists.

![Image 1: Final Destination Bloodlines](https://images.bauerhosting.com/empire/2025/05/final-destination-bloodlines-2.jpg?auto=format&w=1440&q=80)

The precog carnage this time takes place atop a soaring, needle-thin tower not unlike the Stratosphere in Las Vegas, as revellers in the sky-view restaurant stomp their stuff to a band playing ‘Shout’. Iris (Brec Bassinger) is the one being ‘treated’ to a preview, as a rogue coin flung by a bratty kid kickstarts Death’s signature Rube Goldberg routine: champagne corks pop, drums thud, chandeliers tremor, rivets spring, heels scrape, the glass floor cracks, and… well, by the time this extended set-piece finally comes to rest in pieces, chances are the cinema you’re watching it in will be rocking with applause.

But while this thrilling opener is everything you’d expect from a _[Final Destination](https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/final-destination-review/)_ movie, it’s also something different — set in the 1960s. We then crash-cut to the present as Stefani (Kaitlyn Santa Juana) awakens screaming. Plagued by night terrors for two months now, she’s flunking college, her scholarship in doubt. And so she decides to investigate the recurring nightmare. Might the Iris in the dream be her long-lost grandmother?

> So comes the usual Mouse Trap mayhem, all of it splattery fun.

Entertaining as it is, the _Final Destination_ franchise was getting tired when it was [laid to rest in 2011](https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/final-destination-5-review/) — there are only so many times you can rinse and repeat before the Grim Reaper’s scythe gets rusted. This reboot, then, offers a tweak to the format, with the group in peril being not pals and a rando or two, but a family. Searching for answers, Stefani teams up with her younger brother Charlie (Teo Briones), cousins Erik, Bobby and Julia (Richard Harmon, Owen Patrick Joyner, Anna Lore), and estranged mum Darlene (Rya Kihlstedt), only to quickly learn that the family tree is about to be felled.

And so comes the usual Mouse Trap mayhem, all of it splattery fun even if none of it quite reaches the giddy heights of that sustained opener. The gaps between the elaborate death scenes, meanwhile, are dedicated as much to the fractured family resolving differences as to exploring how they might get Death to chill out. It’s hardly _[Secrets & Lies](https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/secrets-lies-review/)_, but the no-name young cast prove likeable enough, and all efforts towards characterisation are appreciated — this is, after all, a franchise built on wafer-thin characters, where what’s inside is only of interest when it’s on the outside, in the gooiest form possible. The best bit of family drama has a major skeleton clatter out of the closet in a manner that’s both funny and clever, sure to wrong-foot fans who have become expert in sifting through the red herrings that make each death in the franchise a guessing game.

In fact, the screenplay, by Guy Busick (_[Scream](https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/scream-2022/)_) and Lori Evans Taylor (_Cellar Door_) from a story by Jon Watts (the Tom Holland _[Spider-Man](https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/spider-man-homecoming-review/)_ trilogy), is smart throughout, and is matched by the peppy direction of Zach Lipovsky and Adam. B. Stein. Their 2018 movie, _Freaks_, one-upped both screen versions of Stephen King’s _Firestarter_ in just how to do a sci-fi horror about a young girl with escalating psychic powers, and the directors here demonstrate a similarly crisp understanding of dog-eared material.

Clearly desiring to hit every base, _Final Destination Bloodlines_ runs through all of the how-to-cheat-death rules that were fitfully established over the first five movies, tosses out Easter eggs with the forceful abandon of giant logs bouncing down a highway, and at last offers an explanation — and a satisfying one, at that — as to why mortician William Bludworth (Tony Todd) is such an expert on Death. Reprising his fan-favourite role from the first, second and fifth instalments, genre icon Todd, who passed away last November, is here visibly ill as he courageously delivers his final performance. He brings pathos to the line, “Life is precious… enjoy every single second,” and the film is dedicated to his memory — still, reflective moments amid the rush of squishing heads, bursting eyeballs and tearing genital piercings.

Laugh as you barf. This fun reboot is crammed with affectionate nods and grisly kills as it bids a fond farewell to Tony Todd. Might it have been called ‘Ultimate Destination’?

11.content:
_Warning: This article contains spoilers for "Final Destination Bloodlines."_

A simple MRI scan can save lives, detecting everything from injuries to cancer and strokes. But, in the world of "Final Destination Bloodlines," released May 16, the machine is just another tool to _take_ lives in the most complicated, gory way possible.

The chaos begins with a wild scheme to cheat death — at a hospital. Two brothers decide that one of them needs to die temporarily and be revived, thus tricking death into skipping over them.

Their idea involves Bobby (Owen Patrick Joyner) intentionally eating nuts, which both the character and actor are [allergic to, causing anaphylaxis](https://www.today.com/health/myths-food-allergies-rcna74159).

But, while the other character, Erik (Richard Harmon), leaves the room, the MRI machine in the background begins to turn on. And, through a series of unpredictable mishaps, the MRI's magnetic field increases in strength.

The scene culminates in a horrific tableau: Erik is sandwiched into the fully powered MRI scanner by the wheelchair Bobby had been sitting in, the chair's metal tubes piercing the skull tattoo on his stomach in a pattern that sneakily references the ["Final Destination 5" poster.](https://www.nbcnews.com/pop-culture/pop-culture-news/see-movie-poster-banned-britain-flna6c9593528)

Meanwhile, Bobby, covered in [hives](https://www.today.com/health/hives-skin-disorder-information-t186231) and [having trouble breathing](https://www.today.com/health/what-does-anaphylaxis-look-mom-raises-awareness-after-child-s-t150503), manages to [use his EpiPen](https://www.today.com/parents/essay/child-food-allergy-stranger-saved-life-rcna101048) in time — only to have his skull impaled by the metal coil from a vending machine that flies into the room.

The MRI scene started, as many of the franchise's characteristically gruesome and complex death scenes do, with a simple question of, "What can we ruin for people?" explain directors Adam Stein and Zach Lipovsky.

"We came up with the idea early on, not knowing how to fit it in the movie," Lipovsky tells TODAY.com, "but we knew that it had a lot of incredible potential to be a horrific scene — so much so that, from the beginning, it was kind of everyone's favorite scene."

But, Lipovsky adds, "we really had to push reality beyond the scientific level make a horror scene out of it." Of course, "in the fun that 'Final Destination' has," he says, "the MRI machine goes into the red extreme level to do some crazy stuff."

The film certainly isn't meant to be a medical documentary. But the most effective "Final Destination" deaths draw from and exploit our [real everyday anxieties](https://www.today.com/health/health/carson-daly-opens-back-surgery-delaying-mri-due-panic-attacks-rcna33235). And the team behind the film took some intentional steps to make it at least a little more plausible, the directors say.

So, just how accurate is that "Final Destination Bloodlines" MRI death scene? We spoke to a few experts to find out.

How do MRI machines actually work?
----------------------------------

An MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scanner, as the name suggests, "is a very strong magnet," Dr. Max Wintermark, chair of the department of neuroradiology at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, tells TODAY.com.

"And that strong magnet aligns the hydrogen protons that we have in the water molecules of our body," he explains.

The human body is made up of about 60% water, Ben Inglis, Ph.D., physicist and manager at the University of California, Berkeley Brain Imaging Center, tells TODAY.com.

And, as you'll remember from high school, a water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms (each of which consists of just one proton) and one oxygen atom, he explains. "So, we have a natural magnetism in our body, it's just exceedingly weak," Inglis says. "In order to see it, we need a very, very strong external magnet."

And that's exactly what the MRI scanner provides.

“When you put a patient in an MRI scanner, all those protons basically align according to the magnetic field,” Wintermark adds. The machine also uses radiofrequency waves to knock those protons out of alignment, he explains. And when they return to alignment, "the body is going to emit a radio frequency wave that we can collect," Wintermark says.

Depending on where those protons are located in the body and what kind of condition a patient has, "the type of wave that is sent back is different," Wintermark explains. And that's how doctors are able to use MRI scanners to get a better look at your internal anatomy.

How strong is the magnet in an MRI machine?
-------------------------------------------

Metal in and around an MRI scanner can be a big problem because of the strength of the magnetic field in the machine.

The strength of a magnetic field is measured in Tesla units. As an example, the strength of the Earth's magnetic field is about 50 microTeslas, Inglis says, noting that the field is even slightly weaker at the equator.

Most MRI machines are 1.5 Teslas or 3 Teslas, meaning they are "much stronger than the earth's magnetic field," Wintermark says. There are a few 7 Tesla MRI scanners in the U.S., Inglis says, as well as one 10.5 Tesla MRI at the [University of Minnesota](https://research.umn.edu/news/u-scientists-scan-worlds-first-105-tesla-human-mri-image) and an 11.7 Tesla MRI at the University of Florida.

Higher Tesla MRI machines can produce higher-quality images. But they're also more expensive, Inglis says, to the tune of $1 million per Tesla and up.

To make the "Final Destination" scene a little more plausible, Lipovsky explains, the team intentionally set the scene at a hospital that was also a research center "so that we could have an MRI machine that can go up to 7 Teslas."

However, note that, unlike in "Final Destination Bloodlines," a real MRI scanner cannot gradually increase in magnetic power, the experts say. Aside from a few specially designed animal MRI scanners that can be run at slightly lower levels, the machine will only run at a single Tesla level. (The magnetic field also will not expand at higher Tesla levels the way it does in the movie, the experts say.)

If there is a change in the strength of the magnetic field at all, it's likely to gradually get weaker, not stronger.

"In order to generate those very strong magnetic fields, you need to cool the coil of wire to extremely low temperatures, and it's actually hard to maintain those low temperatures," Wintermark says. If the temperature gets too warm, the magnetic field can get weaker, leaving you with a 0.1 Tesla scanner instead of 1.5 or 3 Teslas, he says.

![Image 1: Bobby intentionally ate peanuts to give himself an allergic attack while the MRI machine turned on in the background.](https://media-cldnry.s-nbcnews.com/image/upload/t_fit-760w,f_auto,q_auto:best/rockcms/2025-05/final-destination-bloodlines-MRI-scene-zz-250514-02-a349fd.jpg)

Bobby intentionally ate peanuts to give himself an allergic attack while the MRI machine turned on in the background.Eric Milner

What happens if metal goes into an MRI scanner?
-----------------------------------------------

These machines need strong magnetic fields to work properly. So you can probably imagine that it's bad news if metal goes in or near one.

Indeed, MRI accidents do happen — including deadly ones.

In their research, the directors discovered "there are a lot of accidents that happen with MRIs, but usually not with people in them," Stein tells TODAY.com. "Things like oxygen tanks or gurneys get sucked towards MRIs," he says.

For example, a [6-year-old child died](https://abcnews.go.com/US/story?id=92745&page=1) during an MRI scan after being hit by an oxygen tank that flew across the room. In 2022, an [inmate and prison guard were both injured](https://www.abc15.com/news/local-news/investigations/records-az-inmate-prison-guard-stuck-to-mri-machine-at-unregulated-imaging-center) after the inmate was placed in the machine while still wearing metal shackles around her waist. And just last year, a wheelchair was brought into an MRI room and was [pulled sideways into the scanner](https://www-ktvu-com.cdn.ampproject.org/c/s/www.ktvu.com/news/freak-accident-mountain-view-exposes-mri-safety-flaws.amp), nearly missing a patient.

While accidents like these are generally quite rare, "This sort of thing happens more often than you would think," longtime "Final Destination" producer Craig Perry tells TODAY.com.

There are many videos on YouTube of people "cranking the MRI machine" while they tether objects like wheelchairs to the wall, Perry says. The items start "levitating and get pulled toward (the machine)," he adds. "It's really terrifying."

In fact, Inglis is responsible for one of the most popular of those demonstrations, with more than [18 million views on YouTube now](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6BBx8BwLhqg). The video shows loose metal objects, such as a stapler, getting sucked into and thrown around inside a 4 Tesla MRI machine.

"Anything that's made out of steel, especially if it's low-grade steel or iron, will be magnetic," he explains. Other metals, including copper and aluminum, aren't magnetic, but they are conductors of electricity. "So, if you try to move them in the magnetic field, you'll feel the force," he explains.

In [another demonstration](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_93TCvWad8E), he rolls up a $1 bill, turning it into a magnet thanks to its ferromagnetic ink, and shows how it rolls directly into the MRI's magnetic field.

There are safety measures in place for good reason
--------------------------------------------------

These are strong magnets, so it’s important for anyone working around an MRI scanner — as well as the patient, of course — to be checked for metal that might interfere with the field.

“Anything that can be removed is removed,” Wintermark says, including piercings, jewelry and clothing (which might contain metallic dyes). Paper money, which sometimes contains ferromagnetic ink, can also be affected, as Inglis demonstrated in another video.

Patients are also checked for implanted devices, like pacemakers, although modern devices and implants are typically tested to be safe up to at least 3 Teslas, Inglis notes.

It can take a long time for patients to go through all these safety checks at their MRI appointment, Wintermark says, but it's worth it to avoid potentially dangerous consequences — and to ensure that the radiologist gets usable images.

The environment around the scanner can be affected, too, which is why Inglis’s lab is outfitted with instruments made of plastic, wood and aluminum (which isn’t magnetic). “Even my fire extinguishers are made out of aluminum,” he says.

Ultimately, though, the directors want to emphasize just how safe MRI scanners are in reality. Knowing that previous deaths in the series have left strong impressions on consumers, particularly the tanning bed scene in [the third installment](https://www.today.com/popculture/final-destination-3-best-series-wbna11238873), "We debated the ethics of putting (the MRI) scene in the movie (for) a long time," Lipovsky says.

"But the scene was continuously everyone's favorite scene, and so we ultimately decided to put it in the movie," he explains. "But we do want people to go to their MRI appointments. It is actually incredibly safe."

And, unlike some other [common imaging tests](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/ct-scans-may-much-radiation-researchers-say-rcna195198), Inglis notes, an MRI scan does not pose any radiation risks.

That's why, if anything, the scene should be taken as a "cautionary tale," Perry says. "There's a reason why there are all these warning signs," he explains, and if more of us paid a little more attention to our surroundings, we'd "live a much longer and more fruitful life."

Warning: This article contains spoilers for _Final Destination Bloodlines_.

One unexpected scene in [**_Final Destination Bloodlines_**](https://screenrant.com/db/movie/final-destination-6/) has been explained by the directors. The horror sequel, which follows Death hunting down the descendants of the survivors of a disaster at a tower restaurant called Skyview, set up a potential death scene for Erik Campbell (Richard Harmon), only to reveal that he lived due to not being a blood relative of Skyview survivor Iris Campbell (Gabrielle Rose), because his mother had an affair. However, Erik is then given one of the bloodiest [_Final Destination Bloodlines_ deaths](https://screenrant.com/final-destination-bloodlines-deaths-ranked-improbable/) when a malfunctioning MRI machine gorily pulls a wheelchair through his torso.

During an interview with [_Polygon_](https://www.polygon.com/horror/602031/final-destination-bloodlines-ending-explained-directors-spoilers-erik-death), _Final Destination Bloodlines_ directors Zach Lipovsky and Adam Stein shared their perspectives on Erik's death and earlier near-death. They pointed to the line spoken by Tony Todd's character William Bludworth, which is that **"_when you f--k with Death, things get messy_,"** indicating that Erik found himself on Death's list by trying to trigger his brother Bobby's (Owen Patrick Joyner) peanut allergy and then bring him back to life, thereby interrupting the chain and saving the rest of his family.

[✕ Remove Ads](https://screenrant.com/premium/?ref=ad_removal)

However, Stein also reflected on Erik's moment in the tattoo parlor, which involved a chain being hooked to his nose ring, trapping him while the building caught fire. Stein shared their idea that **"_Death has a sense of playfulness_"**and that the scene, which was a major misdirect, showed Death approaching its victims like a fisher who might "_hook the fish and then throw ’em back_." Read the directors' full comments below:

> **Stein:**Tony [Todd] says it: when you f--k with death, things get messy.
> 
> 
> **Lipovsky:**That’s right. That was our answer to that question. Right after he dies, that’s the first line — "Why did he die?" And Kaitlyn’s character [echoes Bludworth]: "When you f--k with Death, things get messy." I think that’s a very good lesson for everyone to remember.
> 
> 
> **Stein:** The other big question is, why does Death hook Erik in the tattoo parlor, when he’s not next? We always liked the idea that Death has a sense of playfulness. Just like a fisherman might catch a fish without intending to kill it, and they’ll hook the fish and then throw ’em back, that’s exactly what Death is doing with Eric in that tattoo parlor scene...
> 
> 
> The thing that makes [Bloodlines] richer as a viewing experience is that in the previous movies, you end up rooting for Death more than you end up rooting for the characters, because Death is so clever, the way he works. His Rube Goldberg magic is so much fun to watch. It’s full of irony and surprises. We wanted to retain that, and really milk all these deaths for all the fun dark comedy.
> 
> 
> But you’re also rooting for the characters, and not wanting them to die. So it gives you both levels of experience at the same time. That really makes it a more complete, more interesting, fun viewing experience for the audience.

Ultimately, the directors' comments confirm what was already present in the screenplay by Guy Busick and Lori Evans Taylor. **The warning given by William Bludworth is more than enough explanation** for Erik's death before the [ending of _Final Destination Bloodlines_](https://screenrant.com/final-destination-bloodlines-ending-explained/) in spite of the fact that he is technically not one of Death's original intended victims.

The late Tony Todd played eerily knowledgable mortician William Bludworth in four of the six _Final Destination_ movies.

[✕ Remove Ads](https://screenrant.com/premium/?ref=ad_removal)

However, by expanding on the reasoning behind Erik's death, they offered further insight into how Death operates in the [_Final Destination_ movies](https://screenrant.com/all-final-destination-movies-ranked/). The playfulness of Death does not generally manifest in the exact way that it does with Erik in _Bloodlines_. However,**there are multiple instances of Death being playful in the previous installments**, including the Rube Goldbergian misdirects that are common in the death sequences and multiple instances of Death letting characters think they have survived for several days, weeks, or even months, before pulling the rug out from under them.

### There Is More To Explore With Death

![Image 12: Erik (Richard Harmon) hanging from a chain while the room is on fire in Final Destination Bloodlines](https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/final-destination-bloodlines-16.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1)

Even though **_Final Destination Bloodlines_**is the sixth installment in a horror franchise that has now run for 25 years, Death's treatment of Erik proves that there are still plenty of new ways for filmmakers to explore the ways the entity operates in the universe of the film series. This, in addition to the movie's stellar box office performance that has seen it become the highest-grossing installment, proves that the [possible _Final Destination 7_](https://screenrant.com/final-destination-7-explained/) should be greenlit, as there is much more ground to cover with Death and its various rampages.
